That is the only place in these four chapters where the string points at Pierre, and it is conditional on a letter that may have been destroyed.

characters.who: The illegitimate son of the dying Count Bezúkhov: a spectacled, blurting young Bonapartist at Anna Pávlovna's soirée in July 1805, and by the end of ch XXIV the silent, uncomprehending object of a fight over the will that is expected to make him one of the richest men in Russia.
timeline: Ch V — Wants to make a remark because the conversation interests him, but Anna Pávlovna, who has him under observation, cuts him off before he can start.
Ch V — Breaks in anyway, blushing, to say almost all the French aristocracy has gone over to Bonaparte; the vicomte answers him without looking at him.

Ch V — Declares the execution of the Duc d'Enghien a political necessity and Napoleon great-souled for shouldering the responsibility. Anna Pávlovna whispers "Dieu! Mon Dieu!" in terror, the little princess asks whether assassination shows greatness of soul, several voices exclaim, and Prince Hippolyte slaps his knee: "Capital!"
Ch V — Looks solemnly at his audience over his spectacles and presses on: the Bourbons left the people to anarchy, Napoleon alone understood the Revolution and quelled it.

Ch V — Twice refuses Anna Pávlovna's offered escape to "the other table", growing more eager, and pushes further: "The Revolution was a grand thing!" — betraying, the narrator says, his extreme youth and his wish to say everything in his mind.

Ch V — Not knowing whom to answer, he looks at them all and smiles; the narrator stops for the set-piece about that smile — grave, even gloomy, replaced instantaneously by a childlike, kindly, rather silly look that seems to ask forgiveness. The vicomte, meeting him for the first time, sees this young Jacobin is not so terrible as his words.

Ch V — Prince Andrew comes to his rescue ("How do you expect him to answer you all at once?"); Pierre chimes in, pleased at the reinforcement. Andrew, having wished to tone down the awkwardness of Pierre's remarks, rises to leave, and Hippolyte's Moscow anecdote is used by the room to bury the outburst.

Ch XXI — Absent, but the whole chapter is about him: Prince Vasíli tells Catiche he has sent for Pierre at the dying count's own demand, that last winter's will leaves everything to Pierre, and that an unsent letter asks the Emperor to legitimize him. Catiche's answer is that Pierre is illegitimate — "un bâtard!" — and cannot inherit.

Ch XXIV — Arrives in the reception room with Anna Mikháylovna. Prince Vasíli and the eldest princess fall silent; Pierre thinks he sees the princess hide something. Vasíli says nothing to him, only squeezing his arm below the shoulder.

Ch XXIV — In the small circular drawing room he remembers sitting there during balls, not knowing how to dance, watching ladies multiplied in the mirrors; now two candles, whispering strangers, and he does not eat although he would very much have liked to.
Ch XXIV — Sees his "monitress" go back on tiptoe to the reception room, concludes that this too is essential, and follows after a short interval.

Ch XXIV — Called into the fight as a witness ("Pierre, my dear, come here... I think he will not be out of place in a family consultation"), he comes quite close and gazes in astonishment at the princess' face, which has lost all dignity, and at Prince Vasíli's twitching cheeks. He says nothing — he speaks not one line in this chapter.
Ch XXIV — The eldest princess comes out of the bedroom, sees him, and turns on him with irrepressible hatred: "Yes, now you may be glad! This is what you have been waiting for."

Ch XXIV — Prince Vasíli staggers out, drops onto the sofa beside him, takes him by the elbow and weeps about sin, deceit and death, with a sincerity and weakness Pierre had never heard in his voice before.

Ch XXIV — Anna Mikháylovna comes out last, kisses his forehead, wets him with her tears and tells him "He is no more." She leads him into the dark drawing room, where he is glad no one can see his face, and returns to find him asleep with his head on his arm.

Ch XXIV — In the morning she tells him he is young and now, she hopes, in command of an immense fortune — but that the will has NOT yet been opened — and asks him to carry out his father's wish about Borís. Pierre is silent, understands nothing of it, colors shyly and looks at her without a word.

characters.who: Maid of honor and favorite of the Dowager Empress Márya Fëdorovna, a forty-year-old St Petersburg hostess whose professional enthusiasm runs the soirée of July 1805 and whose side-business is matchmaking.
timeline: Ch I — July 1805. Suffering, as she says, from la grippe (a new word in St Petersburg, used only by the elite), she has sent out French invitations by scarlet-liveried footman that morning, signed "Annette Schérer."
Ch I — Greets Prince Vasíli Kurágin, the first to arrive, with an attack on Buonaparte, Genoa and Lucca, and a threat to stop being his friend.

Ch I — The narrator fixes her: despite her forty years she overflows with animation and impulsiveness; being an enthusiast has become her social vocation, and she performs it even when she does not feel like it, to avoid disappointing expectations.

Ch I — Bursts out mid-politics with the tirade on Austria's betrayal, Russia alone saving Europe, and the sovereign crushing the hydra of revolution — then suddenly pauses, smiling at her own impetuosity.
Ch I — Advertises the evening's catches: le Vicomte de Mortemart, one of the genuine émigrés, and the Abbé Morio.
Ch I — Refuses to criticize the Empress' wish about Baron Funke, almost closing her eyes; as she names the Empress her face assumes profound devotion mingled with sadness, as it does every time.

Ch I — With courtierlike quickness, rebukes and consoles Vasíli in one move: praises his daughter's coming out, then says she does not like Anatole and that he was mentioned at Her Majesty's and Vasíli was pitied.

Ch I — Proposes the match that starts the novel's marriage plot: Anatole to Princess Mary Bolkónskaya, whose father is rich, stingy, eccentric and nicknamed "the King of Prussia." She mentions in passing that Mary's brother, married to Lise Meinen and an aide-de-camp of Kutúzov's, will be there tonight.
Ch I — Has her hand kissed and swung to and fro; answers "Attendez" and promises to speak to Lise that very evening, calling it her apprenticeship as old maid.
Ch V — Opens the Napoleon argument as hostess, mocking the Milan coronation and hoping this is the last drop that makes the glass run over.
Ch V — Keeps Pierre under observation and interrupts him, speaking for the Emperor Alexander with the melancholy she reserves for the Imperial family, and trying to be amiable to the royalist émigré.
Ch V — Horror-struck at Pierre's defence of the Duc's execution; mutters "Dieu! Mon Dieu!" in a terrified whisper and finds she cannot stop him.
Ch V — Twice offers Pierre the diplomatic exit of "the other table"; twice ignored.
Ch V — Seeing that Pierre's sacrilegious words have not exasperated the vicomte, she rallies her forces and joins the vicomte in a vigorous attack on the orator.
Ch V — Smiles at Hippolyte's unintelligible anecdote and, with the others, appreciates his social tact in so agreeably ending Pierre's unpleasant outburst.

"Prince Andrew" and "Prince Hippolyte" (ch V) — Vasíli does not appear in ch V at all, so no "prince" tag in that chapter is his. Prince Hippolyte is his own son, and the two must not be collapsed.
"Count Bezúkhov" / "the count" — the dying man whose estate he is working on; Vasíli is a prince, and his claim runs through his wife, one of the direct heirs.

"Catiche" / "my dear" / "my poor Catiche" / "my dear Princess Catherine Semënovna" — these are HIS forms of address for the eldest princess. In the long untagged stretches of ch XXI this address asymmetry (he says Catiche, she says mon cousin) is the only thing distinguishing the two speakers.
"the Military Governor of Moscow" (ch XXI) — the visitor Vasíli escorts to the door, described as over sixty; not Vasíli, who is "getting on for sixty" himself.
characters.who: A high-ranking, languid court official who speaks like an actor repeating a stale part, and who spends these chapters working two schemes: a post at Vienna and a rich wife for his sons, and the suppression of the will that would give the Bezúkhov fortune to Pierre.
timeline: Ch I — Arrives first at Anna Pávlovna's reception in embroidered court uniform, knee breeches and shoes, stars on his breast, and complacently seats himself on the sofa after kissing her hand.
Ch I — Says he must appear at the English ambassador's fete; his daughter is coming to fetch him. He flatters by reflex, "like a wound-up clock," saying things he does not even wish to be believed.

Ch I — Asks with studied carelessness whether the Dowager Empress wants Baron Funke as first secretary at Vienna. The narrator immediately exposes it: this was the chief motive of the visit, and Vasíli wants the post for his son. He is rebuffed and falls silent, looking indifferent.

Ch I — Admits his sons are the bane of his life: "Hippolyte is at least a quiet fool, but Anatole is an active one," said with a smile that reveals something unexpectedly coarse round his mouth. Anatole costs him forty thousand rubles a year.

Ch I — Hears the Bolkónskaya proposal, indicates by a movement of the head that he is considering it, asks only whether she is rich, then takes Anna Pávlovna's hand and bends it downwards as is his habit: "Arrange that affair for me... She is rich and of good family and that's all I want."
Ch XXI — At the Bezúkhov deathbed, grown thinner and paler over the last few days, he escorts the Military Governor of Moscow to the door, repeating something to him several times in low tones.

Ch XXI — Alone in the ballroom he sits with his face covered by his hand, then rises, looks about him with frightened eyes, and goes with unusually hurried steps down the long corridor to the room of the eldest princess.

Ch XXI — In her dark room he takes the chair she has just vacated. His cheeks begin to twitch nervously, giving his face an expression never seen on it in a drawing room; his eyes look impudently sly one moment and glance round in alarm the next.

Ch XXI — Lays out the arithmetic: the three sisters, Mámontov and his wife are the count's only direct heirs; he is getting on for sixty and must be prepared for anything; he has sent for Pierre because the count demanded it.

Ch XXI — Reveals the winter will leaving everything to Pierre, and the letter to the Emperor asking for Pierre's legitimation — written, not sent, and known to the Emperor. He cites the family solicitor Dmítri Onúfrich for confirmation.

Ch XXI — Presses her hard: seizes her hand, pulls the little table angrily back, holds her fast when she twice tries to rise, flatters her "excellent heart," insists he came simply to help the count and her.
Ch XXI — Gets exactly what he came for: the paper is in the inlaid portfolio the dying man keeps under his pillow.

Ch XXIV — Discovered in the reception room with the eldest princess under the portrait of Catherine the Great, talking eagerly; they fall silent when Pierre appears. He sends Anna Mikháylovna off to tea and says nothing at all to Pierre.

Ch XXIV — Sits through the women's fight in his familiar attitude, one leg crossed high, wearing the air of a man little concerned in what the two ladies are saying, while his flabby cheeks twitch violently.

Ch XXIV — Rises at last: "this is absurd! Come, let go I tell you." The princess obeys, Anna Mikháylovna does not. He offers to take the responsibility and go ask the dying man himself, then warns her she will answer for the consequences.

Ch XXIV — Bends his head and spreads out his hands when the princess snatches the portfolio; when Anna Mikháylovna carries it into the bedroom, he and the eldest princess recover themselves and follow.

Ch XXIV — Comes out after the death, staggers to the sofa, drops onto it beside Pierre, pale, his jaw shaking as if in an ague, and weeps: "How often we sin, how much we deceive, and all for what? I am near sixty... Death is awful."
Ch XXIV — Afterwards Anna Mikháylovna speaks disapprovingly of his behavior, and of the eldest princess', to the Rostóvs — but in whispers and as a great secret.

characters.who: Kutúzov's aide-de-camp, recently married to Lise Meinen, who spends the soirée quoting Napoleon at the room with a sarcastic smile and then rescues Pierre from it.
timeline: Ch I — Present only by report: Anna Pávlovna mentions Princess Mary's brother, who married Lise Meinen lately, is an aide-de-camp of Kutúzov's, and will be at the soirée tonight. He is never named in this chapter.
Ch V — Looks Anna Pávlovna straight in the face with a sarcastic smile and repeats Napoleon's "Dieu me la donne, gare à qui la touche!", then the same words in Italian.
Ch V — Contradicts his hostess: matters have gone too far and it will be difficult to return to the old regime — pointedly crediting "Monsieur le Vicomte" for the observation.

Ch V — The narrator notes it is evident he does not like the vicomte and is aiming his remarks at him, though without looking at him; he quotes Napoleon again: "I showed them the path to glory, but they did not follow it."
Ch V — Keeps looking with an amused smile from Pierre to the vicomte and from the vicomte to their hostess while the attack on Pierre builds.

Ch V — Intervenes for Pierre: "How do you expect him to answer you all at once?" and offers the distinction that saves the argument — a statesman's acts as private person, as general, and as emperor must be judged separately. He grants Napoleon the bridge of Arcola and the plague hospital at Jaffa, but not everything.
Ch V — Having evidently wished to tone down the awkwardness of Pierre's remarks, he rises and makes a sign to his wife that it is time to go — the exit Hippolyte's anecdote then delays.

characters.who: An impoverished, honey-voiced princess who attaches herself to the dying Count Bezúkhov as his kinswoman, steers Pierre through the deathbed, and wins the physical fight for the portfolio containing the will.
timeline: Ch XXI — Absent but denounced: Catiche names her to Prince Vasíli as "that protégé of yours... the infamous, vile woman" who wheedled herself into the house last winter and told the count such disgraceful things about the sisters, especially Sophie, that he would not see them for a fortnight — which is when, Catiche believes, he wrote the will.

Ch XXIV — Enters the reception room with Pierre; the princess whispers "I can't bear the sight of that woman," and Prince Vasíli sends her off to tea: "Go and take something, my poor Anna Mikháylovna, or you will not hold out."
Ch XXIV — Takes Pierre to the small drawing room, then goes back on tiptoe to the reception room, where she and the princess stand speaking in excited whispers.
Ch XXIV — Blocks the way to the bedroom, blandly but impressively, on the ground that worldly conversation would be too much for poor Uncle when his soul is already prepared.

Ch XXIV — When the princess tries to pass, she springs to bar her path and seizes the inlaid portfolio so firmly it is plain she will not let go easily, begging "Je vous en conjure." Through the struggle her voice loses none of its honeyed firmness and softness.
Ch XXIV — Calls Pierre over as a witness: "I think he will not be out of place in a family consultation; is it not so, Prince?"
Ch XXIV — Refuses Prince Vasíli's order to let go, and is warned she will answer for the consequences; the princess darts at her, shrieks "Vile woman!" and snatches the portfolio away.
Ch XXIV — When Olga bursts out of the bedroom and her sister drops the portfolio, Anna Mikháylovna stoops, quickly catches up the object of contention, and runs into the bedroom with it. She wins.

Ch XXIV — Comes out last, with slow quiet steps, kisses Pierre on the forehead, wets him with her tears, and tells him "He is no more." She leads him into the dark drawing room and leaves him there; when she returns he is asleep.

Ch XXIV — In the morning she tells Pierre he is now, she hopes, in command of an immense fortune, that the will has not yet been opened, and that Uncle promised her only the day before yesterday not to forget Borís but had no time — asking Pierre to carry out his father's wish.

Ch XXIV — Returns to the Rostóvs', goes to bed, and on waking tells them and all her acquaintances an edifying version of the count's death and of the touching last meeting between father and son. Of the behavior of the eldest princess and Prince Vasíli she speaks disapprovingly, but in whispers and as a great secret.

characters.who: The eldest of the three Bezúkhov nieces, stonily severe, straight-backed and varnish-smooth, who knows where the will is and loses it in a physical fight on the threshold of her uncle's death chamber.
timeline: Ch XXI — Found in her own almost dark room at the back of the house: two tiny lamps before the icons, a scent of flowers and burnt pastilles, crowded whatnots and little tables, a high white feather bed behind a screen, and a small dog that begins to bark.

Ch XXI — Prince Vasíli opens the door; she rises and smooths hair so extremely smooth it seems made of one piece with her head and covered with varnish, and asks in fear whether anything has happened.

Ch XXI — Sits down opposite him with her unchanging stonily severe expression, holding the little dog on her lap with thin bony hands, resolved not to be the first to break silence if she has to wait till morning; the narrator gives her a straight rigid body abnormally long for her legs and prominent gray eyes with no sign of emotion.

Ch XXI — Meets the inheritance argument with piety and then with law: "He has made wills enough! But he cannot leave the estate to Pierre. Pierre is illegitimate" — and, smiling as people do who think they know more than their interlocutor, "un bâtard!"

Ch XXI — When Vasíli produces the letter to the Emperor and the solicitor's opinion, a sudden change takes place in her ideas: her thin lips grow white, her voice passes through transitions she herself evidently did not expect, and she pushes the little dog off her lap.
Ch XXI — Erupts about ingratitude — "meanness, deceit, envy, intrigue, and ingratitude—the blackest ingratitude—in this house" — twice tries to rise, and is twice held fast by the hand.
Ch XXI — Names the intriguer: Anna Mikháylovna, whom she would not take for a housemaid, who last winter told the count vile things about them, especially about Sophie, and made him ill.

Ch XXI — Gives up the location: "It's in the inlaid portfolio that he keeps under his pillow," said while ignoring Vasíli's question about why she did not say so sooner, then almost shrieks that if she has a great sin it is hatred of that vile woman.

Ch XXIV — Sitting with Prince Vasíli under the portrait of Catherine the Great, talking eagerly; they break off when Pierre enters, and Pierre thinks he sees her hide something as she whispers "I can't bear the sight of that woman."

Ch XXIV — Has had tea served in the small drawing room (reported by Vasíli), then comes out with the inlaid portfolio in her hand, in the same state of excitement as when she slammed the door of her room, claiming the real will is in the writing table and this is only a paper he has forgotten.

Ch XXIV — Fights Anna Mikháylovna for the portfolio; shrieks at her silent cousin so loudly that the drawing room hears — "Why do you remain silent when heaven knows who permits herself to interfere... Intriguer!" — and tugs with all her might.

Ch XXIV — Obeys Prince Vasíli's "let go" and then breaks: darts unexpectedly at Anna Mikháylovna, shouts "Vile woman!" and snatches the portfolio back — only to drop it when her sister bursts out of the bedroom.

Ch XXIV — Follows the others into the bedroom and comes out a few minutes later with a pale hard face, again biting her underlip. At the sight of Pierre her expression shows an irrepressible hatred: "Yes, now you may be glad! This is what you have been waiting for." She bursts into tears, hides her face in her handkerchief and rushes from the room.

characters.who: The dying grandee of Catherine's court whose sixth stroke, will and unsent letter of legitimation drive chapters XXI and XXIV, and who never speaks a single line in any of the four chapters.
timeline: Ch XXI — Has a sixth stroke while the sixth anglaise is being danced in the Rostóvs' ballroom; the doctors pronounce recovery impossible.

Ch XXI — After a mute confession, communion is administered and preparations are made for the sacrament of unction; his house fills with the bustle and thrill of suspense usual at such moments, and undertakers wait beyond the gates, hiding whenever a carriage drives up, in expectation of an order for an expensive funeral.

Ch XXI — The Military Governor of Moscow, who has been sending aides-de-camp to inquire, comes in person and stays about half an hour alone with him before leaving. It is said in the room that the count no longer recognizes anyone.

Ch XXI — Established by report: last winter he made a will leaving all his property to Pierre rather than to his direct heirs, and wrote — but did not send — a letter to the Emperor asking for Pierre's legitimation; he demanded that Pierre be called; and he keeps an inlaid portfolio under his pillow.

ceiling_note:
WHAT THESE FOUR CHAPTERS ESTABLISH. 225 gold spans across 001/005/021/024: 217 attributed to a named or describable person, 7 left UNKNOWN by the text itself (ch V i4 a broken extractor span, i30 "several voices", i42 "an ironical voice"; ch XXI i4-i7, four anonymous crowd voices), and 1 NOT-SPEECH (ch I i2, the written invitation card signed "Annette Schérer"). Every speaking presence in the four chapters is covered above; the 20 records account for all 217 attributed lines. Speech is heavily concentrated: Prince Vasíli 67, Catiche 38, Anna Pávlovna 31, the vicomte 16, Anna Mikháylovna 13, Pierre 12, Prince Andrew 10, everyone else 8 or fewer.

WHAT THEY DO NOT ESTABLISH — GAPS THE WIKI MUST NOT PAPER OVER.

(1) Line counts here are DIALOGUE PRESENCE, not importance, and the two come apart badly. Count Bezúkhov speaks zero lines and is the subject of two entire chapters. Pierre speaks 12 lines, all of them in ch V, and NOT ONE in ch XXIV — the chapter in which his life changes. His silence is the characterisation; a records table sorted by line count would rank him below the vicomte and hide that.

(2) Two chapters are one continuous scene (I and V are both the July 1805 soirée) and two are another (XXI and XXIV are the same night at the Bezúkhov house). So this is not four samples of a character, it is two. Nobody appears in both settings — Prince Vasíli comes closest, and even he is in I, XXI and XXIV but not V. Anna Pávlovna, Andrew, the vicomte, Hippolyte and Lise exist only in Petersburg; Anna Mikháylovna, Catiche, Lorrain and Olga only in Moscow. Any claim of the form "X and Y know each other" outside these two clusters is unsupported here.

(3) Several canonical names are IMPORTED, and each import is flagged in its record. "Olga" comes from ch XVI and ch XXIII, not from XXI or XXIV. "Hélène" appears nowhere in these four chapters. "Kurágin" is never attached to Hippolyte. "Bolkónski" is never attached to Andrew in ch V, which contains no surnames at all. Count Bezúkhov's given name is never supplied. The ch V "elderly lady" is identified as Princess Drubetskáya only in ch IV, outside this set, so Anna Mikháylovna's presence at the soirée is imported too. A per-chapter gold standard and a cross-chapter character page want different name strings; the alias table should stay separate from the per-chapter attributions rather than being baked back into them.

(4) The endings are provisional in ways a summary tends to over-close. At the end of ch XXIV the will HAS NOT BEEN OPENED — Anna Mikháylovna says so — so Pierre is an expectant heir, not yet Count Bezúkhov. Whether the letter of legitimation survived, who now holds the inlaid portfolio's contents, and what Vasíli does next are all open. Likewise ch I ends with the Anatole/Mary match merely promised to be raised with Lise that evening.

(5) The trap this corpus is densest in is the shared-name problem, and it is not decorative. "Count Bezúkhov" denotes Pierre's father in every occurrence in these chapters but one forecast inside Prince Vasíli's ch XXI speech. "Prince Bolkónski" in ch I denotes Andrew's father, in a sentence a careless reader will attach to Andrew. "The princess" in ch XXI splits between two different women, and in ch XXIV always means Catiche and never Anna Mikháylovna though both are princesses in the same fight. "The doctor" splits between Lorrain and the German. "Catherine" is both Catiche and the Empress in the portrait on the wall. "The King of Prussia" is both a nickname and a monarch inside one chapter. "An aide-de-camp" is Prince Andrew in ch I and an unnamed officer in ch XXI. Each of these is spelled out in the relevant not_variants; a page that merges any one of them is confidently wrong rather than merely incomplete.

(6) Timelines here are event-level and chapter-bounded. They record what the narration says happens to a person inside these four chapters, including offstage report (what Vasíli tells Catiche about the will, what the room says about the count). They do NOT establish backstory, motive beyond what the narrator states, or anything about the ~24 other chapters of Book One that sit between and around them — chapters in which, among other things, Pierre visits his dying father, the eldest princess slams the door referred to in ch XXIV, and Anna Mikháylovna presses Prince Vasíli about Borís.
